1127: Location exerted a highly significant effect on the b* value. The highest value, 113.67, was recorded at Purba Bardhaman, followed by Nadia with 113.14 and Birbhum/Howrah with 111.35. No two locations shared a letter group, each therefore standing apart from the remaining two, and the gap between the superior and inferior sites amounted to 2.32.
1129: The three landraces also differed among themselves, the varietal effect being highly significant. Kalojira recorded the highest value, 113.16, followed by Radhunipagal with 112.64 and Gobindabhog with 112.35. Each landrace occupied a discrete letter group, Kalojira exceeding Gobindabhog by 0.81.
1131: Storage period altered the b* value to a highly significant degree. In order of sampling, the values were 108.35 in fresh paddy, 114.51 at 4 months, 113.94 at 8 months and 114.07 at 12 months, the maximum occurring at 4 months and the minimum in fresh paddy. Over the full year the value increased by 5.3%.
1133: Location and variety did not operate independently, their interaction being highly significant. Kalojira at Purba Bardhaman constituted the superior combination with 115.48, and Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah the inferior one with 109.26. Rank order varied with location: at Nadia the ranking ran Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal, Kalojira; at Purba Bardhaman, Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal; and at Birbhum/Howrah, Radhunipagal, Kalojira, Gobindabhog. Such reordering establishes that the landraces responded to their environments to differing degrees.
1134: The location × storage interaction was highly significant. The highest mean, 115.85, was recorded for Purba Bardhaman at 4 months and the lowest, 105.12, for Birbhum/Howrah in fresh paddy. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change amounted to +1.2% at Nadia, +7.2% at Purba Bardhaman and +7.7% at Birbhum/Howrah, a spread of 6.5 percentage points, with grain from Nadia changing most and that from Birbhum/Howrah least. The rate of change during storage was therefore not uniform across grain of the three provenances.
1135: Variety and storage period did not act independently. The highest mean, 115.00, was recorded for Radhunipagal at 4 months and the lowest, 106.10, for Gobindabhog in fresh paddy. Over the twelve months the change amounted to +7.8% in Gobindabhog, +7.4% in Radhunipagal and +0.9% in Kalojira, Kalojira shifting furthest and Gobindabhog least. The three landraces therefore did not gain or lose at equivalent rates during storage.
1136: The three-way interaction was highly significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 117.48 was recorded by Kalojira grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 4 months, and the minimum of 92.38 by Gobindabhog grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled as fresh paddy, a spread of 25.10. This range appreciably exceeded that generated by any single factor in isolation, the three factors having operated jointly; a favourable outcome therefore required all three to be specified concurrently.
1145: The b* value locates a sample on the blue-to-yellow axis. This outcome is to be expected, since polishing removes the greater part of the coloured bran and the residue differs little between these three landraces. Once curing was complete, b* ceased to shift, which accords with Yanxia et al. (2018), who detected no significant change in the b* value of milled rice during conventional storage. This stability is material, since yellowing is customarily interpreted as evidence of grain deterioration. Genkawa et al. (2008) attributed yellowing to elevated moisture and temperature rather than to the passage of time alone, and Wang et al. (2025) similarly determined that the yellowing rate of newly harvested rice was contingent upon the drying regime rather than upon the subsequent duration of storage.
1149: Location exerted a highly significant effect on the total colour difference. The highest value, 42.29, was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah, followed by Purba Bardhaman with 41.87 and Nadia with 39.69. The three locations resolved into discrete groups, each differing significantly from the others, and the gap between the superior and inferior sites amounted to 2.60.
1151: The landraces likewise differed significantly, the varietal effect being highly significant. Radhunipagal recorded the highest value, 41.42, followed by Gobindabhog with 41.31 and Kalojira with 41.12. Radhunipagal and Gobindabhog shared a common letter and were thus on par with each other, while Radhunipagal exceeded Kalojira by 0.30.
1153: Storage period altered the total colour difference to a highly significant degree. In order of sampling, the values were 27.22 in fresh paddy, 46.08 at 4 months, 45.71 at 8 months and 46.12 at 12 months, the maximum occurring at 12 months and the minimum in fresh paddy. Over the full year the value increased by 69.4%.
1155: The location × variety interaction was highly significant. Radhunipagal at Purba Bardhaman constituted the superior combination with 45.56, and Radhunipagal at Nadia the inferior one with 38.76. The varietal order was not conserved across sites: at Nadia the sequence ran Gobindabhog, Kalojira, Radhunipagal; at Purba Bardhaman, Radhunipagal, Gobindabhog, Kalojira; and at Birbhum/Howrah, Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal. Rank reversal of this order establishes that the landraces responded differentially to the three environments.
1156: The location × storage interaction attained the 1% level. The highest mean, 47.55, was recorded for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months and the lowest, 22.41, for Nadia in fresh paddy. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change amounted to +103.8% at Nadia, +86.4% at Purba Bardhaman and +33.7% at Birbhum/Howrah, a spread of 70.1 percentage points, with grain from Birbhum/Howrah changing most and that from Nadia least. The rate of change during storage was therefore not uniform across grain of the three provenances.
1157: The variety × storage interaction was significant at the 1% level. The highest mean, 46.81, was recorded for Radhunipagal at 4 months and the lowest, 26.08, for Radhunipagal in fresh paddy. Over the twelve months the change amounted to +71.2% in Gobindabhog, +77.2% in Radhunipagal and +60.7% in Kalojira, Kalojira shifting furthest and Radhunipagal least. The three landraces consequently did not gain or lose at equivalent rates during storage.
1158: The three-factor interaction attained the 1% level. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 49.74 was recorded by Radhunipagal grown at Purba Bardhaman and sampled at 8 months, and the minimum of 18.82 by Radhunipagal grown at Nadia and sampled as fresh paddy, a spread of 30.92. No single factor in isolation generated a range of this width; location, landrace and storage acted in combination, and the optimum outcome was attainable only through the appropriate conjunction of all three.
1167: The total colour difference consolidates L*, a* and b* into a single index and affords a convenient measure of the distance of a sample from a reference colour. Birbhum and Howrah returned the largest colour difference at 42.29, followed by Purba Bardhaman at 41.87 and Nadia lowest at 39.69. As this index integrates all three colour readings, its behaviour follows directly from theirs. For the trade the implication is that stored aromatic rice is unlikely to be rejected on colour within a year, provided moisture is held in check. No previous study of this character in these landraces, or of its change during storage, was identified among the literature reviewed in Chapter II, so the present values may be regarded as a first record for the cultivars concerned.
1172: Location exerted a highly significant effect on copper. The highest value, 0.051 ppm, was recorded at Nadia, followed by Purba Bardhaman with 0.035 ppm and Birbhum/Howrah with 0.025 ppm. Each location occupied a discrete letter group, matching neither of the others, and the gap between the superior and inferior sites amounted to 0.026 ppm.
1174: Varietal differences were equally distinct, attaining significance at the 1% level. Kalojira recorded the highest value, 0.039 ppm, followed by Gobindabhog with 0.038 ppm and Radhunipagal with 0.034 ppm. All three landraces were statistically discrete, Kalojira exceeding Radhunipagal by 0.004 ppm.
1176: The effect of storage on copper was non-significant. In order of sampling, the values were 0.037 ppm in fresh paddy, 0.037 ppm at 4 months, 0.037 ppm at 8 months and 0.037 ppm at 12 months, the peak occurring in fresh paddy and the trough at 4 months. The value declined by 0.7% over the year.
1178: The location × variety interaction was significant at the 1% level. Radhunipagal at Nadia constituted the superior combination with 0.059 ppm, and Radhunipagal at Birbhum/Howrah the inferior one with 0.018 ppm. Varietal ranking was not conserved across the three districts: Nadia yielded the order Radhunipagal, Gobindabhog, Kalojira; Purba Bardhaman the order Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal; and Birbhum/Howrah the order Kalojira, Gobindabhog, Radhunipagal. Such rank reversal establishes that the three environments did not act uniformly upon every landrace.
1179: The location × storage interaction was non-significant. The highest mean, 0.052 ppm, was recorded for Nadia in fresh paddy and the lowest, 0.024 ppm, for Birbhum/Howrah likewise in fresh paddy. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change amounted to -3.3% at Nadia, -0.4% at Purba Bardhaman and +4.5% at Birbhum/Howrah. The magnitude of change was comparable across locations, storage having been conducted at a single site and having acted uniformly on grain of every provenance.
1180: Variety and storage did not interact significantly. The highest mean, 0.040 ppm, was recorded for Kalojira at 8 months and the lowest, 0.033 ppm, for Radhunipagal at 8 months. Across twelve months Gobindabhog changed by -0.6%, Radhunipagal by -0.3% and Kalojira by -1.2%. None of the three shifted appreciably more than the others, and no differential response to storage was detected among them.
1181: The three-factor interaction was non-significant. Among the thirty six treatment combinations, the maximum value of 0.060 ppm was recorded by Radhunipagal grown at Nadia and sampled at 4 months, and the minimum of 0.018 ppm by Radhunipagal grown at Birbhum/Howrah and sampled at 8 months. Given the non-significance of this term, these extreme cells cannot be interpreted as genuine differences in isolation, and the main effects afford the more reliable inference.
1190: Copper is required in small quantities in the human diet, and rice supplies a proportion of that requirement. Grain mineral content is determined during the growing season, when the roots absorb the element and the plant translocates it into the developing grain. The observed difference therefore derives from the copper status of the three soils and from the chemical conditions governing its availability to the plant. The spread of 0.005 ppm is exceedingly narrow, indicating that landrace exerts far less influence over copper than does the soil. Reports on these minerals in the aromatic landraces of West Bengal remain scarce. Singh et al. (2022) recorded wide cultivar differences in mineral content among the pigmented rices of north-east India, and Naveed et al. (2023) observed that the ash and mineral contents of brown Basmati remained stable through six months of storage while the antioxidant fraction declined, which corroborates the mineral stability observed here.
1194: Location exerted a highly significant effect on iron. The highest value, 0.481 ppm, was recorded at Birbhum/Howrah, followed by Nadia with 0.227 ppm and Purba Bardhaman with 0.171 ppm. All three locations were statistically discrete, differing significantly among themselves, and the gap between the superior and inferior sites amounted to 0.309 ppm.
1196: Varietal differences were equally distinct, attaining significance at the 1% level. Gobindabhog recorded the highest value, 0.525 ppm, followed by Radhunipagal with 0.224 ppm and Kalojira with 0.130 ppm. All three landraces were statistically discrete, Gobindabhog exceeding Kalojira by 0.395 ppm.
1198: The effect of storage on iron was non-significant. In order of sampling, the values were 0.293 ppm in fresh paddy, 0.293 ppm at 4 months, 0.294 ppm at 8 months and 0.292 ppm at 12 months, the maximum occurring at 8 months and the minimum at 12 months. A decline of 0.5% was registered over the full year.
1200: The location × variety interaction was highly significant. Gobindabhog at Birbhum/Howrah constituted the superior combination with 1.338 ppm, and Radhunipagal at Birbhum/Howrah the inferior one with 0.049 ppm. The landraces did not retain the same order at every location: the order at Nadia was Radhunipagal, Kalojira, Gobindabhog; at Purba Bardhaman, Radhunipagal, Gobindabhog, Kalojira; and at Birbhum/Howrah, Gobindabhog, Kalojira, Radhunipagal. Rank reversal of this kind indicates a differential response to the growing environment.
1201: No significant interaction arose between location and storage. The highest mean, 0.482 ppm, was recorded for Birbhum/Howrah at 4 months and the lowest, 0.169 ppm, for Purba Bardhaman at 12 months. Between fresh paddy and 12 months of storage the change amounted to -1.2% at Nadia, -1.8% at Purba Bardhaman and +0.4% at Birbhum/Howrah. All three locations shifted by closely comparable margins, the effect of storage proving independent of the district of origin.
